# Raising for Long Cycles

Source: https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Long-cycle companies raise against milestones, not time. Build a capital stack that mixes dilutive, non-dilutive, strategic and project money, each matched to the risk it can carry, and show investors one retired risk per round. With a median two years between seed and Series A, runway has to cover the full sales cycle plus the next raise.

Long-cycle companies raise against milestones, not time. Build a capital stack that mixes dilutive, non-dilutive, strategic and project money, and show investors one retired risk per round. The 2026 data supports the approach: hardware funding on Carta's platform nearly doubled in the first half of the year, but non-dilutive programmes proved slow and conditional, and US project lenders say plainly that they will not fund pilots.

*This is commercial advice about how to run a raise, not investment advice.*

## Why the standard round does not fit

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) said raise against evidence. [Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) said run the round like a sales process. Both hold. What changes in emerging tech is the clock.

A software company can close customers inside a twelve-month runway. A robotics, compute or energy company often cannot. The pilot alone may take a year. Procurement adds another. Revenue arrives after the money has gone.

So the round cannot be sized to time. It has to be sized to the next thing that makes the company worth more. That is a milestone, and the whole raise is built around naming it.

Investors are in the category. Carta's first-half 2026 data shows hardware capital rising from $8.6 billion to $14.3 billion year on year, and energy from $1.2 billion to $2.2 billion, while seed capital overall fell from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion. The money is going to companies that can show a step, not to category stories at seed.

## The capital stack for long cycles

No single source carries a long-cycle company. The stack is layered, and each layer has a job.

| Source | What it funds well | What it costs | 2026 reference point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Milestone-based equity | The next de-risking step | Dilution, board seats | Median seed to Series A gap of two years (Carta) |
| Grants and public funding | Research, early prototypes, pilots in regulated sectors | Reporting, slow timelines, restrictions on use | SBIR reauthorised to 2031 after a six-month lapse; EIC Accelerator grants up to €2.5 million from TRL 6 |
| Strategic investors | Capability the corporate needs | Information rights, possible exclusivity pressure | Corporate venture arms in 82.6% of US deal value (PitchBook) |
| Ecosystem and foundation funds | Work that strengthens a shared protocol or network | Alignment with the ecosystem's priorities | Varies by ecosystem |
| Project finance | Proven assets with contracted cash flows | Lender conditions, requires a proven model first | US federal energy loans prefer TRL 8 and contracted cash flows |

Non-dilutive money goes first where it exists. It is slow, and the reporting is real, but it funds the work investors will not pay for yet. The slowness is not hypothetical. The Congressional Research Service records that US SBIR and STTR programmes, which obligated $4.4 billion and $662.3 million in awards in fiscal 2022, lost their authority for six months before the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act was signed on 13 April 2026. The new law extends them to 30 September 2031 and adds Strategic Breakthrough awards of up to $30 million, which must be matched dollar for dollar by new private capital or other funds. In Europe, the EIC Accelerator offers grants of up to €2.5 million covering 70% of development costs from technology readiness level 6, with equity of up to €10 million for market entry, across six cut-off dates in 2026.

Strategic investors are useful when they need what you build. A corporate with a hard operational problem is a better partner than one running an innovation theatre. Check whether their ask is a cheque or a controlling relationship.

Project finance belongs later. It funds the hundredth unit, not the first. Mayer Brown's August 2026 guide to the US Office of Energy Dominance Financing, formerly the Loan Programs Office, notes a preferred technology readiness level of 8, that research, pilot and demonstration projects will be denied, that loans cannot exceed 80% of eligible project costs, and that direct loans are typically $500 million or more. Using equity to build hardware that project finance could fund is a common and expensive mistake. Using equity because project finance will not yet fund it is the correct choice.

## What investors want to see per milestone

Each round should retire one named risk. Investors in long-cycle companies look for three kinds of proof, roughly in order.

| Proof | What it looks like | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Technical de-risking | A deployment that survived a month at the customer's scale and conditions | A demo |
| A paying pilot | A customer with a budget put money against the problem | A free pilot, which is evidence of interest |
| Regulatory clearance | Permission to operate near a utility, a government or a regulated buyer | An application with no date |

Free pilots are evidence of interest. Paid pilots are evidence of pain. For climate, energy, identity and anything near a utility or a government, permission is a milestone in itself. It is also a moat, because the next entrant has to earn it too.

Name the milestone this round funds. Name the one after it. An investor who can see two steps ahead will fund one.

> Free pilots are evidence of interest. Paid pilots are evidence of pain.

## Runway maths when sales cycles run twelve to twenty-four months

Start from the sales cycle, not from the burn. If the cycle is eighteen months, the first paying customer closes eighteen months after first contact, at best. Pipeline built today pays in the round after next.

That means the current round must fund the company through the whole cycle, plus the time to raise again. Eighteen months of cycle plus six months of raise is two years of runway, minimum. Most founders raise for twelve. The market timetable agrees with the arithmetic: Carta's first-quarter 2026 data puts the median gap at two years from seed to Series A and 2.1 years from Series A to Series B, across all sectors.

Three practical rules. Model revenue starting at month eighteen, not month six. Model pilots as cost, not income, until they convert. Model the next raise as a six-month project that starts when the milestone lands, not when the cash runs out.

[Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) said the system should run without the founder. Here that includes a finance function that tracks milestone progress against cash, monthly, so the raise starts on time. The discipline is the same one a sales team uses for [forecasting that holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/): dated commitments, stage evidence and no credit for hope.

## Narrative discipline: two slides

The deck has one job on slide one and a different job on slide two.

Slide one is the category. Why it will exist, why now, why it is large. This is where the investor decides whether to care.

Slide two is the next eighteen months. The milestone this round funds, the proof you will have, and what that proof makes possible. This is where the investor decides whether to write a cheque.

Most emerging tech decks are all slide one. They sell the future and never show the step. Investors who have seen a hundred category stories want to know what changes by next year.

Keep the claims register from [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) beside the deck. Every number on slide two should trace to a line in it. [Revenue models for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/revenue-models-for-long-cycles/) covers how to price the pilots and contracts that slide two promises.

## lowob takeaways

- **Size the round to a milestone.** Name the one it funds and the one after.
- **Match each layer of capital to the risk it can carry.** Grants for research, equity for de-risking, project finance for proven units.
- **Plan for slow public money.** Apply early and keep a fallback if a programme pauses.
- **Fund the whole cycle plus the next raise.** Two years is the floor when the cycle is eighteen months.

## Common questions

### How much runway does a deep tech or hardware startup need?

Start from the sales cycle, not the burn. An eighteen-month cycle plus six months to raise again means two years of runway minimum. Carta's 2026 data puts the median gap between seed and Series A at two years.

### What funding sources should a long-cycle company use?

A layered stack: milestone-based equity, grants and public funding such as SBIR or the EIC Accelerator, strategic investors, ecosystem and foundation funds, and later project finance for proven assets with contracted cash flows.

### Can a startup use project finance for a first deployment?

Rarely. US federal energy lenders prefer technology at readiness level 8 and deny research, pilot and demonstration projects. Project finance funds units of a proven design with contracted cash flows.

### What do investors want to see in each round of a long-cycle company?

One retired risk per round: technical de-risking in a real deployment, a paying pilot, or regulatory clearance. Paid pilots are evidence of pain; free pilots are evidence of interest.

## Next move

Write the milestone this round funds and the one after it on one page. Then list every non-dilutive programme you qualify for, with its next deadline, and model the runway as if none of them pays out on time.
